name: Malleswaram (Malleshwaram)
description: One of Bengaluru's oldest neighbourhoods and its 'cultural heart', Malleswaram is a dense north-central residential locality laid out on a rectilinear grid of 1st and 8th Main Roads. It is anchored by the 17th-century Kadu Malleshwara Temple and by a busy street market that supplies the whole north of the city with oil, millets and provisions. The area also holds the Indian Institute of Science and, at its southern edge, the World Trade Center Bengaluru.
history: The area was conquered by Shahaji Bhonsle, a general of the Bijapur Sultanate, during the first half of the 17th century, and Ekoji I, Shahaji's son, donated the village of Medaraninganahalli - near today's Indian Institute of Science - to the Kadu Malleshwara Temple. Inscriptions dated 1669 call the locality 'Mallapura', and a Kannada inscription found near Sampige Road is recorded in Epigraphia Carnatica. The name was absent from British records: the Survey of India in 1878 placed the site inside Ranganathapalya village. In 1889 Maharaja Chamaraja Wodeyar X appointed a committee headed by K. Seshadri Iyer to relieve congestion in central Bengaluru; that committee planned Malleshwaram and Basavanagudi, with Malleshwaram initially covering 291 acres. The committee ended in 1895, when the municipality incorporated the neighbourhood into Bengaluru, and growth was initially slow - during the 1896 plague epidemic health authorities set up camps and medical tents here, and many of the survivors settled permanently.
facts: Inscriptions dated 1669 call the locality 'Mallapura'; the Kadu Malleshwara Temple itself dates to 1669 CE and is built in the Dravidian style.
The Kadu Malleshwara Temple was built in 1669 by Venkoji, identified as the step-brother of the Maratha king Shivaji; the deity is Shiva worshipped as Mallikarjun.
The neighbourhood was planned by the 1889 K. Seshadri Iyer committee, which also laid out Basavanagudi, and initially covered 291 acres.
The committee was wound up in 1895 when the neighbourhood was incorporated into Bengaluru; during the 1896 plague epidemic the area hosted camps and medical tents for infected patients.

The locality covers 3.95 km2 with a population of 99,625 (2020), and contains the Indian Institute of Science, the Institute of Wood Science and Technology and the World Trade Center Bengaluru, described as the city's tallest commercial building.
The Kadalekai Parishe groundnut fair is held in Malleshwaram and Basavanagudi every November; in 2025 the Malleshwaram leg ran 8-10 November and more than 200 groundnut vendors took part.

name: Basavanagudi
description: Basavanagudi is a residential and commercial locality in south Bengaluru, named after the Bull Temple whose monolithic Nandi gives the place its name - 'basava' means bull and 'gudi' means temple in Kannada. DVG Road runs through it as the neighbourhood's commercial spine, and midway along that road the Gandhi Bazaar market opens into a dense lane of flower, fruit and vegetable stalls. The locality also holds B.M.S. College of Engineering and the century-old Vidyarthi Bhavan restaurant.
history: Basavanagudi is described as one of the oldest and 'poshest' localities of Bangalore, a status evidenced by four inscriptions in the neighbourhood, three in Kannada and one in Tamil, and by the 1537 Bull Temple built by Kempe Gowda during the Vijayanagara Empire. Development was guided by the same 1889 K. Seshadri Iyer committee that planned Malleswaram, which laid out Basavanagudi in the same period as a residential quarter south of the old Pete. The commercial spine grew along DVG Road, where several of the retail businesses date back to the 1920s and 1930s; Vidyarthi Bhavan, the neighbourhood's best-known vegetarian restaurant, opened in 1943, and B.M.S. College of Engineering was established in 1946.
facts: The Bull Temple was built in 1537 by Kempe Gowda in Vijayanagara style; its present vimana was added in the early 20th century and decorated with Saivite figures and motifs.

The temple's monolithic granite Nandi stands on a plinth, blackened by repeated applications of charcoal and oil, and measures about 15 ft (4.6 m) high and 20 ft (6.1 m) long - among the world's largest Nandi images.
The locality is home to four inscriptions, three in Kannada and one in Tamil.
B.M.S. College of Engineering was established in 1946 and is credited as the first private engineering college in India.
Vidyarthi Bhavan, the vegetarian restaurant on the DVG Road, opened in 1943.
Wikipedia's locality infobox records a population of 32,640 for the Census of 2011; PIN codes are 560004, 560019, 560028 and 560050.

name: Jayanagar
description: Jayanagar is south Bengaluru's flagship planned neighbourhood, laid out in 1948 on the model of New Delhi and divided into ten numbered blocks. Its Kannada name combines 'Jaya' and 'nagar' - literally 'Victory City'. Most blocks are residential villas and apartment blocks, while the 3rd and 4th Blocks are the commercial core, home of the Jayanagar Shopping Complex and the district's busiest market street.
history: The foundation of Jayanagar was laid in 1948, making it one of Bengaluru's earliest planned neighbourhoods and, at the time, one of the largest in Asia. Before the city's expansion, Jayanagar marked the southern limit of the urban area - the historic South End Circle and the Ashoka Pillar were the boundary markers, with 'South End' still used for the district. The layout was divided into ten blocks numbered 1 to 9 plus a fourth 'T' block, and it was later divided into seven wards. The Jayanagar BDA Shopping Complex opened in 1976 with the Puttanna Kanagal theatre inside; a fire in 2008 damaged it, and redevelopment beginning around 2011-12, at a cost of roughly 193 crore rupees, included demolishing the theatre.
facts: The foundation was laid in 1948 and the neighbourhood was among Asia's largest planned neighbourhoods at the time.
Jayanagar is divided into ten blocks - Blocks 1 to 9 plus a fourth 'T' block - with the 3rd and 4th Blocks largely commercial and the rest residential.
The Jayanagar BDA Shopping Complex opened in 1976 and contained the Puttanna Kanagal theatre.
A fire in 2008 damaged the shopping complex; redevelopment beginning around 2011-12 cost roughly 193 crore rupees and included demolition of the theatre.
The locality comprises seven wards and had about 180,000 voters in 2013.
South End Circle and the historic Ashoka Pillar marked Jayanagar as the traditional southern limit of the city.

name: Indiranagar
description: Indiranagar is an east-central locality that began as a bungalow suburb and became one of Bengaluru's most commercialised districts after the IT boom. Its two spine corridors - 100 Feet Road and CMH Hospital Road - carry high-end fashion stores, bars and pubs, while the side streets remain a low-rise residential quarter of independent houses.
history: Indiranagar was formed as a Bangalore Development Authority layout in the late 1970s and was named after M. K. Indira. It started as a suburb of bungalows and detached houses and became more commercial after Bengaluru's late-1990s IT boom; it is now both an important residential and a commercial hub. 100 Feet Road and CMH Hospital Road became the commercial corridors, with BMTC bus routes running along CMH Road, 80 Feet Road and 100 Feet Road and 12th Main Road serving the 100 Feet Road corridor. The Purple Line of the Namma Metro serves the area through the Indiranagar and Swami Vivekananda Road stations.
facts: The locality was created as a BDA layout in the late 1970s and named after M. K. Indira.
100 Feet Road and CMH Hospital Road became the commercial corridors after the late-1990s IT boom, drawing high-end fashion stores, bars and pubs.
BMTC routes use CMH Road, 80 Feet Road and 100 Feet Road, with 12th Main Road a stop on the 100 Feet Road route.
The Purple Line of the Namma Metro serves the area through the Indiranagar and Swami Vivekananda Road stations.
Kempegowda International Airport lies approximately 35-40 km away, normally 45-60 minutes by road.

name: Koramangala
description: Koramangala is a south-east Bengaluru locality of tree-lined roads, bungalows and low-rise apartments that became a commercial centre and a prominent startup hub during the technology boom. It is laid out in eight blocks that straddle the Inner Ring Road, which separates Blocks 1-4 from Blocks 5-8. The 80 Feet Road corridor links the blocks and carries the neighbourhood's restaurants, cafes and offices.
history: Koramangala was planned as a suburban area after independence; until the 1970s travellers commonly bypassed it, and housing expanded in the late 1970s. Its position between Bengaluru and Electronic City attracted migrants from across India during the city's technology boom in the late 1990s, when it transformed into a major commercial and business destination. The eight blocks cover roughly 1,800 acres, with the Inner Ring Road separating Blocks 1-4 from Blocks 5-8. The neighbourhood's rise coincided with Electronic City's growth as an IT hub, with companies such as Infosys based there.
facts: Koramangala is divided into eight blocks covering roughly 1,800 acres, with the Inner Ring Road separating Blocks 1-4 from Blocks 5-8.
Planned as a suburban area after independence, it was bypassed by travellers until the 1970s, with housing expanding in the late 1970s.
The locality's growth was driven by migration from across India during the late-1990s technology boom, and it is now described as a commercial centre and a prominent startup hub.

name: Mahatma Gandhi Road (M. G. Road)
description: Mahatma Gandhi Road is the principal commercial spine of central Bengaluru, running east-west between Trinity Circle and Anil Kumble Circle past Cubbon Park, M. Chinnaswamy Stadium and the CBD junctions. It is lined continuously with retailers, eateries, restaurants, offices, shops, theatres and banks, and is categorised as an Indian shopping district. Two Namma Metro stations - Mahatma Gandhi Road and Trinity - serve the corridor.
history: The road was known as 'South Parade' before independence and was renamed Mahatma Gandhi Road on 26 February 1948. It has since become the city's busiest high-street, and the building of the Namma Metro beneath and along it required a full reconstruction of the boulevard. The Mahatma Gandhi Road metro station opened for service on 20 October 2011.
facts: The road was renamed Mahatma Gandhi Road on 26 February 1948; it was previously known as South Parade.
It extends between Trinity Circle and Anil Kumble Circle in central Bengaluru.
The corridor has two Namma Metro stations, Mahatma Gandhi Road and Trinity; the Mahatma Gandhi Road station opened for service on 20 October 2011.
The boulevard was reconstructed following the construction of the metro.
Wikipedia categorises M. G. Road as an Indian shopping district and describes it as lined with retailers, eateries, restaurants, offices, shops, theatres and banks.
Cross streets and nearby landmarks include Cubbon Road, Dickenson Road, St. Marks Road, Residency Road and Brigade Road.

name: Brigade Road
description: Brigade Road is one of central Bengaluru's busiest retail districts, running north-south from M. G. Road down to Hosur Road with links en route to Residency Road and Church Street. It contains shopping centres, bookstores, international-brand stores, cafes, restaurants and pubs, and it is a long-established city celebration venue with fairy lights strung across the road for New Year.
history: Brigade Road grew as the retail spine of the British-era central business district, and it retains several of its colonial and early-20th-century civic buildings - St. Patrick's Church, the Bengaluru Opera House and the Sapper War Memorial, the latter a First World War memorial to fallen members of the Madras Sappers & Miners (Madras Engineer Group). The Opera House was later leased to Samsung and rebranded as the Samsung Opera House, functioning as an experience centre and store. The street also became a marker of modern retail change: India's first KFC branch opened on Brigade Road in June 1995.
facts: Its north end is M G Road and its south end is Hosur Road; it is a one-way link with links en route to Residency Road and Church Street.
Landmark buildings include St. Patrick's Church, the Bengaluru Opera House and the Sapper War Memorial, a First World War memorial to the Madras Sappers & Miners.
The Opera House was leased to Samsung and rebranded the Samsung Opera House, now an Experience Centre and store.
India's first KFC branch opened on Brigade Road in June 1995.
In 2004 parking meters were imported from France for 85 parking spaces, with an average of 1,400 cars reportedly parked there each day.
The street has its own bus station and is reachable from the M G Road metro station on the Namma Metro Purple Line.

name: Church Street
description: Church Street is a 750-metre pedestrian-scale retail street in the central business district, running from Brigade Road to St. Mark's Road alongside M. G. Road. Named for St. Mark's Cathedral, which it leads to, it is a principal shopping and nightlife destination and a popular New Year's Eve gathering point. It was the first Bengaluru street to be paved with granite cobblestones and briefly became a motor-free pedestrian street.
history: Church Street took its name from St. Mark's Cathedral, toward which the street leads. Redevelopment works costing 9 crore rupees began in 2017, laying granite cobblestones that made it the first Bengaluru street paved this way, in a 'Kasuti' arrangement intended to evoke Karnataka's cultural heritage. In 2020 the street was closed to motor vehicles under the 'Clean Air Street' trial, with outdoor seating, cultural programmes and buggies or e-rickshaws for disabled people and senior citizens; the trial ended on 31 May 2021. A bomb blast on the street on 14 May 2014 killed one person and injured four, with authorities suspecting the Indian Mujahideen.
facts: The street runs 750 metres from Brigade Road to St. Mark's Road alongside M G Road.
It is named for St. Mark's Cathedral, toward which the street leads.
2017 redevelopment works cost 9 crore rupees; the granite cobblestone 'Kasuti' paving made it the first Bengaluru street paved this way.

During the 2020 'Clean Air Street' trial, average daily footfall rose 92%, peak-period footfall rose 117%, more than half of establishments reported higher revenue, and 98% of surveyed users liked the pedestrianised street; the Indian Institute of Science monitored the trial.
The pedestrian trial ended on 31 May 2021; the stated reason was transfer to the BBMP, although the BBMP denied receiving instructions to continue.
An IED blast on the street in 2014 killed one person and injured four others, with authorities suspecting the Indian Mujahideen.

name: Commercial Street
description: Commercial Street is one of the oldest and busiest shopping areas of the city, running between OPH Road and K. Kamraj Road in the Tasker Town part of the central business district, with shopping continuing into bylanes such as Dispensary Road and Abrahim Sahab street. It trades in clothes, footwear, jewellery and electronics and is among the city's most crowded streets.
history: Commercial Street sits inside the old Pete, the market core laid out by Kempegowda I in 1537 around a mud fort, with roads running to the cardinal directions and gates at their ends. The street's retail character dates from the colonial era, when the cantonment and the Pete markets were linked by a busy thoroughfare; photographs of the street survive from 1900 and from the Eid celebrations of 2012. The area's growth was never formally planned, and commerce has spread from the main carriageway into the surrounding bylanes.
facts: It runs between OPH Road and K. Kamraj Road, with associated shopping continuing into bylanes such as Dispensary Road and Abrahim Sahab street.
Wikipedia describes it as 'one of the oldest and busiest shopping areas of the city'.
Principal goods include clothes, footwear, jewellery and electronics, alongside numerous food establishments.
The street is among the city's most crowded, with only 75 four-wheeler parking spaces reported.
Archival photographs exist of Commercial Street in 1900 and during Eid in 2012.
It lies in the Shivajinagar / Tasker Town quarter of the central business district, near M G Road and Russell Market.

name: Majestic (Kempegowda Bus Station)
description: Majestic is the transport hub of Bengaluru, centred on the Kempegowda Bus Station opposite the KSR Bengaluru railway station. The at-grade complex handles both intercity KSRTC services and intracity BMTC buses, and is bounded by Seshadri Road, Danavanthri Road, Tank Bund Road and Gubbi Thotadappa Road. The Nadaprabhu Kempegowda, Majestic metro station on the Purple and Green lines sits directly above it.
history: The bus station was first known as Majestic, after a nearby cinema theatre, and was later named for Kempe Gowda I; Majestic remains the most familiar name. Construction began in 1965 and the intercity station opened in 1969. The semicircular city-bus terminal was added in the 1980s, with the intracity section dated to 1980, and former Karnataka chief minister R. Gundu Rao is credited with developing the station. The site had formerly held Dharmambudhi Lake, which dried up in the early twentieth century. In 2025 Chief Minister Siddaramaiah announced redevelopment of the complex under the Project Majestic public-private-partnership scheme.
facts: Construction began in 1965 and the intercity station opened in 1969; the semicircular city-bus terminal was added in the 1980s, with the intracity section dated to 1980.
The station was initially known as Majestic after a nearby cinema theatre, and was later named for Kempe Gowda I.
It is an at-grade integrated complex with four intracity bays and four intercity terminals, handling BMTC city buses and KSRTC intercity services.
Wikipedia lists 61 intracity platform designations and 16 intercity platform designations.
The site formerly contained Dharmambudhi Lake, which dried up in the early twentieth century; former chief minister R. Gundu Rao is credited with developing the station.
In 2025 Chief Minister Siddaramaiah announced redevelopment of the complex under the Project Majestic public-private-partnership scheme.

name: Whitefield
description: Whitefield is an east Bengaluru suburb that began as an Anglo-Indian agricultural settlement in 1882 and is today one of the city's principal IT corridors. The Export Promotion Industrial Park and International Tech Park (ITPL) form the business core, ringed by large residential apartment clusters that grew rapidly after 2002. It is also served by the Purple Line metro extension to Whitefield (Kadugodi) and by an electrified double-track railway line to Chennai.
history: The locality began in 1882 as an agricultural settlement for Eurasians and Anglo-Indians, when Mysore's Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X granted 3,900 acres (16 km2) to the Eurasian and Anglo-Indian Association; it was named for David Emmanuel Starkenburgh White, president of the association and a promoter of the settlement. In the first decade of the 1900s Whitefield had about 45 houses, including 18 on the village site, and around 2,000 acres (8.1 km2) of cultivable land, with 130 residents recorded in 1907. A railway station was built about 3 km south of the settlement on the Bangalore-Madras line, drawing workers from the Kolar Gold Fields roughly 50 km to the east, with regular trains to Bangalore about 20 km west. Whitefield stayed a small village until the late 1990s, when Bengaluru's technology boom transformed it into a major suburb, with residential construction surging from the latter half of the 1990s and particularly from 2002.
facts: The settlement was founded in 1882 when Maharaja Chamarajendra Wadiyar X granted 3,900 acres (16 km2) to the Eurasian and Anglo-Indian Association.
It was named for David Emmanuel Starkenburgh White, president of the association and a promoter of the settlement.
In the first decade of the 1900s there were about 45 houses (18 on the village site), roughly 2,000 acres (8.1 km2) of cultivable land, and 130 residents in 1907.
A railway station was built roughly 3 km south of the settlement on the Bangalore-Madras line, attracting workers from the Kolar Gold Fields about 50 km east.

The Export Promotion Industrial Park and International Tech Park (ITPL) became major technology centres, with offices including Mercedes-Benz's R&D centre, Caterpillar at RMZ NXT and Societe Generale.
The Purple Line extension from Krishnarajapura to Whitefield (Kadugodi) runs 13.71 km with 13 intermediate stations; it was inaugurated on 25 March 2023 and opened to passengers on 26 March 2023.

name: Jayanagar 4th Block
subcategory: Commercial block within a residential locality
description: Jayanagar 4th Block is the principal commercial block of Jayanagar, centred on the Jayanagar Shopping Complex and its surrounding street market. It serves as the shopping district for the whole of south Bengaluru, with clothing, footwear, bags, jewellery and food stalls strung along the main cross. The Green Line Jayanagar metro station serves the 4th and 7th Blocks.
history: The block was laid out with the rest of Jayanagar when the neighbourhood was planned in 1948, but became the district's commercial centre with the opening of the Jayanagar BDA Shopping Complex in 1976, which contained the Puttanna Kanagal theatre. A fire in 2008 damaged the complex; redevelopment beginning around 2011-12, at a cost of roughly 193 crore rupees, included demolishing the theatre. The 3rd and 4th Blocks remain the two principally commercial blocks of the locality, while the other blocks are residential.

name: Gandhi Bazaar
description: Gandhi Bazaar is a traditional street market midway along DVG Road in Basavanagudi, and one of Bengaluru's oldest trading areas. It is known for flower, condiment, fruit, vegetable and cloth stalls and for its old eating houses, and it swells with crowds at festivals when shoppers buy puja items. The Kannada writer Masti Venkatesha Iyengar lived here.
history: Gandhi Bazaar sits in the heart of Basavanagudi, the residential quarter laid out in the 1880s by the K. Seshadri Iyer committee alongside Malleswaram. DVG Road, which runs through the bazaar, forms Basavanagudi's commercial centre and contains some of the city's oldest business outlets, several dating back to the 1920s and 1930s. The bazaar's character as a conservative, traditional market quarter was reinforced by the presence of long-standing residents such as Masti Venkatesha Iyengar, and by the century-old vegetarian restaurant Vidyarthi Bhavan, which opened in 1943 nearby.
facts: Gandhi Bazaar lies in Basavanagudi, midway along DVG Road, and is described as one of Bengaluru's oldest areas and a traditional, conservative one.
The Kannada writer Masti Venkatesha Iyengar lived in the bazaar.
Stalls sell fresh flowers, condiments, fruit, vegetables and cloth, alongside numerous restaurants.
The bazaar generally operates from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., with larger crowds during festivals when shoppers buy puja items.
DVG Road forms Basavanagudi's commercial centre and contains some of the city's oldest business outlets, several dating to the 1920s and 1930s.
The Vidyarthi Bhavan restaurant, in the same neighbourhood, was established in 1943.

name: Russell Market
description: Russell Market is a shopping market in the Bangalore Cantonment area of central Bengaluru, named after the municipal commissioner of the period. Built by the British and inaugurated in 1933, it is the city's best-known formal market building, with a predecessor market documented in photographs of the 1880s. Its location puts it between the Church Street and Commercial Street retail district and the government quarter around Cubbon Park.
history: The market was built in 1927 by the British and inaugurated in 1933 by Ismail Sait, and named for the then municipal commissioner T. B. Russell. An archival photograph shows the predecessor market in the 1880s, with the spire of St. John's Church visible behind it. The market's covered blocks survived into the modern era but burned on 26 February 2012, when a fire gutted 123 shops and caused losses of 89.2 lakh rupees; the initial investigation attributed the blaze to a short circuit.

name: Chickpet (Chickpete)
description: Chickpet is one of Bengaluru's oldest commercial districts and the centre of the city's wholesale cloth trade. It occupies the eastern part of the old Pete, where the historic east-west axis of Chikkapet Street meets the north-south axis of Doddapet Street - today Avenue Road - at Doddapete Square. It has one of the smallest arterial roads in the entire city and is noted for the density of its marigold and jasmine garland sellers.
history: Chickpet's roots go back to the 16th century. It is said that Shivaji spent his early childhood in Bengaluru with his father Shahaji Raje Bhosale, and that Shivaji's palace stood in the area now known as Chikkapete. Chickpet formed part of the Pete that Kempegowda I founded in 1537 around a mud fort, its principal east-west axis being Chikkapet Street. The district's commercial identity is textile: within the Pete it was historically associated with textiles, and the broader Pete traded in flowers, grain, bangles, oil, paper, stone and copper vessels by quarter. Chickpet retains the second largest Marwadi community in South India after Sowcarpet in Chennai.
facts: Chickpet's roots go back to the 16th century; Shivaji is said to have spent his childhood in Bengaluru with his father Shahaji Raje Bhosale, and his palace stood in the area now called Chikkapete.
It is one of the city's oldest areas and is famous for its cloth shops and wholesale businesses.
Chikkapet Street was the Pete's principal east-west axis; its junction with the north-south Doddapet Street became Doddapete Square, associated with today's Avenue Road.
The locality reportedly contains one of the smallest roads to serve as an arterial road in the entire city.
Chickpet has the second largest Marwadi community in South India, after Sowcarpet in Chennai.

name: KR Market (Krishnarajendra Market)
description: Krishnarajendra Market - also called City Market - is the largest wholesale market dealing with commodities in Bengaluru, sitting in the Kalasipalya area beside Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace where Mysore Road meets Krishnarajendra Road. Fruit and vegetable stalls occupy the basement and lower ground floor of the main building, with flowers and dry goods above. It is also known as one of the biggest flower markets in Asia.
history: The market was established in 1928 on a site that had earlier been a water tank and an 18th-century battlefield during the Anglo-Mysore Wars, and it was named after Krishnarajendra Wodeyar, a former ruler of the princely state of Mysore. The area is associated with Asia's first electric streetlights: Bengaluru lit them in August 1905, and Wikipedia's article on the market records it as the first locality in the whole of Asia to get electricity. Two British-era buildings survive on the site, one at the front and another at the rear; between them a three-storey concrete structure was built during the 1990s.
facts: The market was established in 1928 and named after Krishnarajendra Wodeyar, a former ruler of the princely state of Mysore.
Before the market, the site was reportedly a water tank and later an 18th-century battlefield during the Anglo-Mysore Wars.

Two British-era buildings survive, one at the front and another at the rear, with a three-storey concrete structure built between them in the 1990s.

The basement holds underground parking; above it are flower and vegetable stalls on the lower ground floor, dry goods on the upper ground floor, and tools and machine-tool accessories on the first floor.

name: Avenue Road (Doddaneedu Street)
description: Avenue Road is a busy shopping and commercial street in Chickpet, central Bengaluru, linking Mysore Road with K. G. Road near Majestic bus station and Bangalore City railway station. Traditionally associated with used books, garments and textiles, jewellery and pawn brokering, it is the wholesale cloth centre of the old city and the main north-south axis of the Pete, running on toward Krishnarajendra Road.
history: The street was earlier known as Doddapete - the name Doddaneedu is the Kannada form of the same word - and its name literally means 'Road Road'. It formed the Pete's principal north-south commercial axis, running from Mysore Road to Krishnarajendra Road and meeting the east-west Chikkapet Street at Doddapete Square; the Pete itself was founded in 1537 by Kempegowda I around a mud fort, with roads laid out to the cardinal directions and gates at their ends. Two illustrated views dated 1890 show the Canarese Chapel and the 'Main Street of the Pettah'. Rice Memorial Church still stands on the road, on the former grounds of the London Mission Canarese Chapel, established in 1834 by William Campbell, and commemorates Rev. Benjamin Holt Rice.
facts: The road was earlier known as Doddapete, and its name literally means 'Road Road'.
It lies in Chickpet, linking Mysore Road and K. G. Road, near Majestic bus station and Bangalore City railway station.
It is traditionally associated with used books, garments and textiles, jewellery and pawn brokering, and forms the Pete's principal north-south commercial axis running on to Krishnarajendra Road.

Rice Memorial Church stands on Avenue Road, on the former grounds of the London Mission Canarese Chapel established in 1834 by William Campbell, and commemorates Rev. Benjamin Holt Rice, a London Missionary Society missionary and Kannada scholar.
Two illustrated views dated 1890 show the Canarese Chapel and the 'Main Street of the Pettah'.
A Hanuman temple stands at the road's entrance.
